title: A Silence for the Blue Hour
premise: Marguerite Okonkwo, a translator in her forties who has spent decades shedding her mother's Igbo like a coat she never chose, finds a bundle of undelivered letters behind a wardrobe in the Lagos house she has returned to after her mother's death. The letters, written by her mother to an aunt who died before they could be sent, reveal a hidden sister given away at birth and a marriage built on silences Marguerite inherited without knowing. As she translates each letter back into the language she is losing, she must decide whether to find the sister, Adaora, now living abroad as someone else entirely. In the end, Marguerite mails the final letter—her own—and meets Adaora at the airport not as family reclaimed but as two strangers choosing, at last, to belong to each other.
about_author: Edmund Okonkwo is the pen name of a Nigerian-British writer who worked for years as a court interpreter in London before turning to fiction. His writing explores the quiet violence of assimilation and the languages families keep losing on purpose.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She sorts through her late mother's Lagos house, translating contracts by day and speaking to neighbors in a halting Igbo that embarrasses them both. She notices how fluently the housekeeper grieves while she herself feels like a lodger. Emotional beat: estrangement disguised as competence.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, flashback woven through present. A memory of age nine, when her mother corrected her English accent one week and punished her Igbo the next. Back in the present, she loses the word for 'threshold' mid-conversation. Emotional beat: grief for a language still technically alive.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Moving the wardrobe to fix a warped floorboard, she finds a biscuit tin of letters, all addressed to 'Nneka Nwosu, Enugu,' none posted, spanning 1971 to 1989. Her mother's handwriting grows shakier across the decades. Emotional beat: the shock of discovering a deliberate archive of silence.

chapters.title: First Letter: 1971
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Marguerite reading, then slipping into her mother Chinyere's voice within the letter itself. A young widow writes of a newborn daughter 'given to God' during the war's aftermath, asking her aunt to intercede with a husband who refused to look at the child. Emotional beat: tenderness curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: The Photograph with Two Girls
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Among her mother's papers she finds a studio photograph of two girls, one clearly herself, one unfamiliar, dated 1978. Her father, visiting briefly from Abuja, goes quiet and leaves early. Emotional beat: the first crack in the official version of her childhood.

chapters.title: Interpreter, Defendant
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV at work. Translating a custody hearing in London-returned files, she watches a mother lie through her interpreter and realizes she has spent her life doing the same for Chinyere. She misrenders a sentence deliberately, then can't sleep. Emotional beat: loyalty and truth pulling apart inside her profession.

chapters.title: Letters of the Middle Years
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Marguerite and letter-Chinyere. The letters track money sent secretly to Enugu, a girl called Adaora growing up in photographs described but never enclosed. Marguerite cross-references dates with her own childhood memories of unexplained absences. Emotional beat: retroactive recognition.

chapters.title: What the Housekeeper Knows
chapters.summary: Housekeeper Ngozi's POV. Ngozi remembers the madam burning papers one harmattan and keeping others; she recognized the tin's hiding place because she dusted around it for thirty years. She tells Marguerite only that 'some doors are locked from both sides.' Emotional beat: complicity of servants in family myths.

chapters.title: The Word for Sister
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Searching online archives, she finds an Adaora Nwosu, now a nurse in Manchester, listed in a diaspora newsletter. She drafts seven emails and deletes them all, unable to write 'your sister' or 'my mother' without lying about something. Emotional beat: paralysis of the translator with no neutral words.

chapters.title: Father's Version
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Emeka Okonkwo, the father, in Abuja. He admits he knew, insists the war excused everything, and warns Marguerite that digging up Adaora will only make 'two ruined daughters instead of one finished one.' Emotional beat: a man defending silence as protection.

chapters.title: Undelivered
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She discovers why the letters were never posted: the aunt died in 1989, and Chinyere kept writing anyway, the last letters addressed to no living person—a diary in epistolary drag. Marguerite understands she is reading her mother talking to herself. Emotional beat: devastating intimacy.

chapters.title: The Blue Hour
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Insomniac, she sits on the veranda each evening between daylight and dark, when the house turns blue and Igbo comes to her effortlessly—the hour her mother used to sing. She begins translating the letters aloud just to hear the language work again. Emotional beat: mourning becoming practice.

chapters.title: Adaora, Elsewhere
chapters.summary: Adaora's POV, first appearance. In Manchester, a woman who answers to 'Dora Nowell' receives a LinkedIn message from a stranger claiming shared blood. She dismisses it, then digs out the only artifact of her origins: a cloth wrapper and a note in a language she cannot read. Emotional beat: suspicion shading into hunger.

chapters.title: Rising Action: The Translation
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She decides to translate every letter into English and send them to Adaora unasked—an act she recognizes as either gift or ambush. Her father threatens to cut her off; her London clients drop her for missed deadlines. Emotional beat: commitment at rising cost.

chapters.title: Letter 1984: The Naming
chapters.summary: Chinyere's letter-voice dominant. She writes of watching Adaora's school photos arrive yearly, of naming her privately on each birthday, of the day she saw her once across a market and did not speak. Marguerite reads it standing up, unable to sit. Emotional beat: the mother as both betrayer and fellow prisoner.

chapters.title: Contact
chapters.summary: Alternating Marguerite/Adaora POV. Adaora finally replies with one line: 'How do I know you're not a scam?' Marguerite sends the photograph of the two girls. A long silence follows, then a voice memo—Adaora speaking accented, half-remembered Igbo learned from a grandmother. Emotional beat: two strangers testing a bridge.

chapters.title: The Confrontation
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, climax begins. At her father's Abuja home, she lays the letters on his table and demands he hear them read aloud in Igbo. He walks out; her brother accuses her of exhuming the dead for content. Marguerite reads alone to an empty room, voice breaking on the word for 'forgive.' Emotional beat: truth spoken at maximum cost.

chapters.title: Climax: What Marguerite Cannot Translate
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The final letter, undated, contains no revelations—only Chinyere asking forgiveness from a daughter she believed would never read it, and naming Marguerite as the one who should decide whether Adaora ever learns the truth. Marguerite realizes the archive was left for her deliberately. Emotional beat: the weight of being made executor of a betrayal.

chapters.title: Decision at the Blue Hour
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. On the veranda, she drafts and burns three versions of a letter to Adaora, then writes the true one: everything, including her own years of willing blindness. She chooses disclosure over the family's peace, mailing the packet with her return address. Emotional beat: agency seized from inheritance.

chapters.title: Arrival
chapters.summary: Adaora's POV. Adaora lands in Lagos having told no one, carrying the wrapper cloth. The sisters meet at arrivals and fail to recognize each other until Marguerite speaks a sentence of Igbo their mother used to sing. They stand awkwardly, neither hugging, both staying. Emotional beat: belonging chosen rather than claimed.

chapters.title: Two Daughters, One Language
chapters.summary: Alternating sisters' POV. Over ten days in the house, Adaora asks questions Marguerite can't answer and Marguerite teaches words Adaora half-knows; together they assemble Chinyere from fragments, less a verdict than a portrait. Ngozi cooks for three and says nothing, which says everything. Emotional beat: reconciliation without absolution.

chapters.title: A Silence for the Blue Hour
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, coda. She posts the last letter—to her mother, care of the blue hour—at the post office that never delivered the others, and lets it go wherever undelivered things go. Speaking Igbo now without apology, she and Adaora plant frangipani where the wardrobe stood. Final beat: silence transformed from erasure into room made for what remains.
